blocks.html: The Engineering Council is the UK’s regulatory body for the engineering profession. It operates under a Royal Charter and is governed by a Board that represents UK Licensees as well as individuals from industries and sectors with an interest in regulation of the profession.

subsections.title: The purpose of the Regulations for Registration

blocks.html: This document is the Regulations for Registration (RfR).
blocks.text: This document is the Regulations for Registration (RfR).

blocks.html: The primary purpose of RfR is to set out the Regulations that Licensees of the Engineering Council must adhere to when registering applicants, recognising programmes of learning and development, and undertaking related processes.
blocks.text: The primary purpose of RfR is to set out the Regulations that Licensees of the Engineering Council must adhere to when registering applicants, recognising programmes of learning and development, and undertaking related processes.

subsections.title: Who the Regulations for Registration are for

blocks.html: Licensees use this document to ensure their processes meet the requirements of their licence.
blocks.text: Licensees use this document to ensure their processes meet the requirements of their licence.

blocks.html: The Engineering Council’s Quality Assurance Committee and its licensing function use this document to support the regular licence reviews of Licensees.
blocks.text: The Engineering Council’s Quality Assurance Committee and its licensing function use this document to support the regular licence reviews of Licensees.

blocks.html: Throughout the Regulations, ‘Licensee’ means an organisation licensed by the Engineering Council Board to assess individuals for professional registration. To become a Licensee, an organisation must demonstrate to the satisfaction of the Engineering Council Board that it is competent to perform this function and regulate the conduct of its members.
blocks.text: Throughout the Regulations, ‘Licensee’ means an organisation licensed by the Engineering Council Board to assess individuals for professional registration. To become a Licensee, an organisation must demonstrate to the satisfaction of the Engineering Council Board that it is competent to perform this function and regulate the conduct of its members.

blocks.html: Additionally, Licensees can be licensed to recognise programmes of learning and competence development to specific standards.
blocks.text: Additionally, Licensees can be licensed to recognise programmes of learning and competence development to specific standards.

blocks.html: Licensees are sometimes known informally as Professional Engineering Institutions, or PEIs.
blocks.text: Licensees are sometimes known informally as Professional Engineering Institutions, or PEIs.

blocks.html: These definitions apply throughout these Regulations.
blocks.text: These definitions apply throughout these Regulations.

blocks.html: A peer is a professionally registered individual whose experience and training enable them to make an informed professional judgment about the professional review, programme recognition, or other matters.
blocks.text: A peer is a professionally registered individual whose experience and training enable them to make an informed professional judgment about the professional review, programme recognition, or other matters.

blocks.html: A peer review is an assessment in which one or more peers consider appropriate evidence against defined requirements and make a documented professional judgment.
blocks.text: A peer review is an assessment in which one or more peers consider appropriate evidence against defined requirements and make a documented professional judgment.

blocks.v44: v4.4 para 22 (new clause built from it)
blocks.html:
Where these Regulations require peer review, Licensees must ensure that:

  • each peer is suitably qualified and trained for the role;
  • at least one peer has appropriate and relevant engineering experience, sufficient to make an informed judgment on the matter being assessed; and
  • all reasonable steps are taken in the selection of peers to ensure that potential conflicts of interest are avoided.

blocks.html: The committee responsible for registration is the body appointed by a Licensee to oversee its registration activity and make or authorise decisions on applications for registration.
blocks.text: The committee responsible for registration is the body appointed by a Licensee to oversee its registration activity and make or authorise decisions on applications for registration.

blocks.html: A committee responsible for recognition is the body appointed by a Licensee to oversee its programme-recognition activity and its accreditation of IPD schemes, and to make or authorise decisions on the recognition of programmes and the accreditation of schemes. This may be one and the same as the committee responsible for registration.

blocks.v44: v4.4 para 25 (third sentence) and para 41 (second sentence)
blocks.html: Engineering Council registrants must be in the majority on the committee responsible for registration and on the committee responsible for recognition.
blocks.text: Engineering Council registrants must be in the majority on the committee responsible for registration and on the committee responsible for recognition.

blocks.html: Recognition is the umbrella term for approval and accreditation.
blocks.text: Recognition is the umbrella term for approval and accreditation.

blocks.html: Approval of a programme of learning attests to its content: its overall design, depth and range of coverage, and the validity and reliability of the assessment of the learner.
blocks.text: Approval of a programme of learning attests to its content: its overall design, depth and range of coverage, and the validity and reliability of the assessment of the learner.

blocks.html: Accreditation confirms that the delivery of a programme of learning, or of an IPD scheme, is recognised at a specific site or sites, or at a specific provider. Accreditation incorporates approval: if delivery is accredited, approval of the underlying content is implicit.

blocks.html: A joint board is a single decision-making body established by two or more Licensees to recognise programmes on their behalf, such as the Joint Board of Moderators.
blocks.text: A joint board is a single decision-making body established by two or more Licensees to recognise programmes on their behalf, such as the Joint Board of Moderators.

blocks.html: A joint visit is an accreditation visit carried out by two or more Licensees together, each of which makes its own recognition decision.
blocks.text: A joint visit is an accreditation visit carried out by two or more Licensees together, each of which makes its own recognition decision.

blocks.html: An interim registrant is a person whose underpinning knowledge and understanding have been assessed as meeting the Standard, but who has not yet demonstrated the necessary competence for final-stage registration.

blocks.html: A final-stage registrant is a person who has successfully completed the Professional Review and holds registered status that is not interim.
blocks.text: A final-stage registrant is a person who has successfully completed the Professional Review and holds registered status that is not interim.

blocks.html: These Regulations for Registration are published by the Board of the Engineering Council and govern the implementation by Licensees of the UK Standard for Professional Engineering Competence and Commitment (UK-SPEC) and related Recognised Standards, and the registration of individuals under those Standards.

blocks.html: Nothing in these Regulations overrides obligations placed on the Engineering Council and Licensees by national and international legislation, including any requirement to process applicants holding recognised international qualifications or credentials.

blocks.html: The Board of the Engineering Council may add to, amend, or revoke paragraphs in these Regulations, on the recommendation of the Registration Standards Committee, or may delegate responsibility for amendment to that committee. Any such changes will be communicated to all Licensees.

blocks.html: The Engineering Council publishes guidance on the professional review, recognition of learning, and other areas covered by these Regulations. The standing of each type of Engineering Council publication is set out in the Code of Practice on Document Hierarchy and Associated Language.

blocks.html: Licensees must submit their application of these Regulations to audit by the Engineering Council’s Quality Assurance Committee (QAC), including the licence reviews set out in the Regulations for Licensing. Licensees must maintain sufficient records for external audit purposes, and must have a suitable management system and self-assessment process in place, in order to demonstrate and maintain conformity with the Engineering Council requirements.

sections.title: Professional registration and the Professional Review

blocks.html:
Competence and commitment will be developed through a combination of:

  • underpinning knowledge and understanding;
  • professional development and experience.
blocks.text: Competence and commitment will be developed through a combination of: underpinning knowledge and understanding; professional development and experience.

blocks.html: Licensees assess an applicant’s underpinning knowledge and understanding before, or alongside, the Professional Review of their competence and commitment. An applicant cannot be awarded final-stage registration until the required underpinning knowledge and understanding have been demonstrated (UKU-001). The stages of assessment, and the gate between each, are summarised in Table 1.
blocks.text: Licensees assess an applicant’s underpinning knowledge and understanding before, or alongside, the Professional Review of their competence and commitment. An applicant cannot be awarded final-stage registration until the required underpinning knowledge and understanding have been demonstrated (UKU-001). The stages of assessment, and the gate between each, are summarised in Table 1.

blocks.html: UK-SPEC and the ICTTech Standard are Prescribed Standards of the Engineering Council. They set out the competence and commitment required for each category of registration, and are the standards against which Licensees assess applicants.

blocks.html: Proprietary Standards and Derived Standards are collectively described as ‘Recognised Standards’. Further detail is set out in the Guidance Note on Recognised Standards.
blocks.text: Proprietary Standards and Derived Standards are collectively described as ‘Recognised Standards’. Further detail is set out in the Guidance Note on Recognised Standards.

blocks.html: Licensees must establish procedures for assessing applicants for registration against UK-SPEC. A Licensee may instead adopt its own standard of competence and commitment, derived from and fully meeting UK-SPEC or a Proprietary Standard, which can be assessed objectively and which relates to the technologies and applications with which it is concerned, provided the standard has been authorised by QAC as a Derived Standard.
blocks.text: Licensees must establish procedures for assessing applicants for registration against UK-SPEC. A Licensee may instead adopt its own standard of competence and commitment, derived from and fully meeting UK-SPEC or a Proprietary Standard, which can be assessed objectively and which relates to the technologies and applications with which it is concerned, provided the standard has been authorised by QAC as a Derived Standard.

blocks.html: Recognised Standards may make requirements of the assessment and revalidation of applicants additional to those in UK-SPEC and these Regulations. Licensees’ processes for assessing applicants for registration and revalidation must comply with any such requirements. Individuals holding registration against a Proprietary Standard may transfer to a corresponding Principal Register category without further assessment, subject to meeting any discipline-specific requirements of the registering Licensee.

Licensees’ processes for assessing applicants for registration and revalidation must comply with any such requirements. Individuals holding registration against a Proprietary Standard may transfer to a corresponding Principal Register category without further assessment, subject to meeting any discipline-specific requirements of the registering Licensee.

blocks.html: Licensees must only register persons who have demonstrated the competence and commitment appropriate to a registration category, and only in categories they are licensed to register. An individual may hold final-stage registration in more than one category of the Register only in exceptional circumstances, whether with one Licensee or more. Guidance about the exceptional circumstances is available. Where an individual seeks such registration with the same Licensee, the Licensee must consider the case individually and assess the applicant against each category independently.

blocks.html: The initial assessment is a clerical check to confirm that an application is complete and that the evidence submitted is genuine. For example, confirming a qualification’s recognised status on the Engineering Council’s recognised programmes database, or verifying certificates. The initial assessment is not peer review; it ensures the application is ready for peer review.

blocks.html: The committee responsible for registration is responsible for the initial assessment and may delegate it to staff. Any delegation to staff must be on the basis of clear procedures and guidance established by the committee, and must be subject to internal audit under the self-assessment process required by V5-003.

blocks.html:
The Licensee must tell applicants what documentation is required, and in what format. This may include their:

  • career history;
  • education and training record; and
  • any evidence of experiential, or on-the-job, learning.

The Licensee must take reasonable steps to verify that the evidence submitted is authentic, is the applicant’s own work, and accurately represents their knowledge, experience and achievements.

Where the Licensee considers that additional evidence of knowledge and understanding, or of competence and commitment, is required, it must tell the applicant what further evidence is needed.

sections.title: Assessment of underpinning knowledge and understanding

blocks.html: Underpinning knowledge and understanding provide the foundation for competent professional practice. Licensees determine whether each applicant has demonstrated the underpinning knowledge and understanding required for the category of registration sought.
blocks.text: Underpinning knowledge and understanding provide the foundation for competent professional practice. Licensees determine whether each applicant has demonstrated the underpinning knowledge and understanding required for the category of registration sought.

blocks.html: Licensees must establish procedures for assessing underpinning knowledge and understanding by each of the methods they accept. Where an assessment requires a professional judgment, rather than the verification of a recognised qualification, it must be made by peer review (V5-074).
blocks.text: Licensees must establish procedures for assessing underpinning knowledge and understanding by each of the methods they accept. Where an assessment requires a professional judgment, rather than the verification of a recognised qualification, it must be made by peer review (V5-074).

blocks.html: The applicable Engineering Council Knowledge Benchmark is the reference against which Licensees must determine whether each applicant’s underpinning knowledge and understanding meet the requirement, including applicants who hold a recognised programme. Where the evidence leaves a gap, Licensees must use the Knowledge Benchmark to identify it.
blocks.text: The applicable Engineering Council Knowledge Benchmark is the reference against which Licensees must determine whether each applicant’s underpinning knowledge and understanding meet the requirement, including applicants who hold a recognised programme. Where the evidence leaves a gap, Licensees must use the Knowledge Benchmark to identify it.

blocks.html:
Underpinning knowledge and understanding may be developed through any appropriate method or combination of methods. In making its determination, a Licensee may consider evidence including:

  • recognised qualifications or programmes of learning;
  • other formal qualifications or programmes of study;
  • work-based or experiential learning;
  • in-employment education and training;
  • self-directed learning;
  • technical reports or other technical evidence;
  • technical interviews, presentations, examinations or other appropriate assessment methods;
  • relevant existing Engineering Council registration; or
  • any combination of these.

In making its determination, a Licensee may consider evidence including: recognised qualifications or programmes of learning; other formal qualifications or programmes of study; work-based or experiential learning; in-employment education and training; self-directed learning; technical reports or other technical evidence; technical interviews, presentations, examinations or other appropriate assessment methods; relevant existing Engineering Council registration; or any combination of these.

blocks.html: Regardless of how underpinning knowledge and understanding are developed or demonstrated, Licensees must satisfy themselves that the applicant’s knowledge and understanding are sufficient, relevant and applicable to their engineering practice.
blocks.text: Regardless of how underpinning knowledge and understanding are developed or demonstrated, Licensees must satisfy themselves that the applicant’s knowledge and understanding are sufficient, relevant and applicable to their engineering practice.

blocks.html: Licensees may accept completion of a recognised programme as evidence of the underpinning knowledge and understanding required, provided they have satisfied themselves that it meets the requirement for the category of registration sought (UKU-001). Where it meets the requirement only in part, UKU-008 applies.

Where it meets the requirement only in part, UKU-008 applies.

blocks.html:
Where a Licensee relies on a recognised programme as evidence of underpinning knowledge and understanding, it must ensure that:

  • the level of the recognised programme held matches or exceeds the level of registration sought by the applicant; and
  • the programme is relevant to the engineering discipline(s) covered by the Licensee.
blocks.text: Where a Licensee relies on a recognised programme as evidence of underpinning knowledge and understanding, it must ensure that: the level of the recognised programme held matches or exceeds the level of registration sought by the applicant; and the programme is relevant to the engineering discipline(s) covered by the Licensee.

blocks.html: The Engineering Council may enter agreements with overseas bodies on mutual recognition of recognised qualifications following consultation with Licensees.
blocks.text: The Engineering Council may enter agreements with overseas bodies on mutual recognition of recognised qualifications following consultation with Licensees.

blocks.html: Licensees must treat such qualifications as equivalent to accredited UK qualifications for registration purposes, subject to UKU-004 and UKU-006.
blocks.text: Licensees must treat such qualifications as equivalent to accredited UK qualifications for registration purposes, subject to UKU-004 and UKU-006.

blocks.html:
Licensees must inform applicants of the outcome of the assessment of their underpinning knowledge and understanding. Where the requirements of the Knowledge Benchmark have not been demonstrated in full, Licensees must:

  • identify the outstanding requirements and tell the applicant what they are;
  • provide the applicant with an appropriate opportunity to demonstrate them through additional evidence or assessment; and
  • ensure that any additional assessment is reasonable and proportionate to the requirements that remain to be demonstrated.

blocks.html: Licensees may use a technical report, technical interview, presentation, examination or other appropriate assessment method where additional assessment is necessary to determine whether an applicant has demonstrated the required underpinning knowledge and understanding.
blocks.text: Licensees may use a technical report, technical interview, presentation, examination or other appropriate assessment method where additional assessment is necessary to determine whether an applicant has demonstrated the required underpinning knowledge and understanding.

blocks.html: A Licensee may ask an applicant to submit a technical report as a means of demonstrating knowledge and understanding. This report must demonstrate that the applicant has the knowledge and understanding necessary to underpin the UK-SPEC competences for the category of registration sought. Its content must be technical; a pure management study is not acceptable.
blocks.text: A Licensee may ask an applicant to submit a technical report as a means of demonstrating knowledge and understanding. This report must demonstrate that the applicant has the knowledge and understanding necessary to underpin the UK-SPEC competences for the category of registration sought. Its content must be technical; a pure management study is not acceptable.

blocks.html: The technical report must be assessed by peer review (V5-074). The assessors of the report and the interview must be two registrants, suitably qualified and trained to assess underpinning knowledge and understanding. An IEng or CEng applicant whose technical report is assessed as satisfactory must proceed to a technical report interview. A report of the technical report assessment may be made available to the Professional Review assessors. While the Professional Review Interview may take place back-to-back with the technical report assessment interview, the two processes must be separately identified and documented.

blocks.html:
Licensees must maintain sufficient records of:

  • the evidence considered;
  • any additional assessment undertaken;
  • the determination reached;
  • any outstanding requirements identified; and
  • the outcome communicated to the applicant.

blocks.html: Licensees may admit applicants to the Interim Section of the Register where they have determined that the applicant has demonstrated the underpinning knowledge and understanding required for the relevant registration category, but has not yet met all requirements for final-stage registration. An individual must not be registered in both the final-stage and interim sections of any one category of the Register.

blocks.html: Interim registration should be awarded for a defined period. Licensees must have arrangements for reviewing an applicant's status at the end of that period and determining whether Interim Registration should be renewed or allowed to expire.
blocks.text: Interim registration should be awarded for a defined period. Licensees must have arrangements for reviewing an applicant's status at the end of that period and determining whether Interim Registration should be renewed or allowed to expire.

blocks.html: Licensees must assess the competence and commitment of every applicant for registration, in any registration category, through a Professional Review conducted by the Licensee through which they are applying for registration.
blocks.text: Licensees must assess the competence and commitment of every applicant for registration, in any registration category, through a Professional Review conducted by the Licensee through which they are applying for registration.

blocks.html:
The Professional Review must include two components:

  • a review of documentary evidence; and
  • an interview.

Licensees may add other components to the Professional Review.
blocks.text: The Professional Review must include two components: a review of documentary evidence; and an interview. Licensees may add other components to the Professional Review.

blocks.html: The application, supporting documentation and interview must be in English, subject only to the provisions of the Welsh Language Act 1993. Another language may be used purely for the clarification of a word or point, to enable the interview to continue.

blocks.html: Licensees must interview all applicants for final-stage CEng or IEng registration, except those exempted under V5-072; and may interview EngTech and ICTTech applicants at their discretion.

blocks.html: Following consultation with Licensees, the Engineering Council may enter into agreements with overseas bodies on mutual recognition of overseas titles, or authorise agreements made by Licensees. The scope of each agreement, and the exemptions it gives, are set out in the agreement itself. A list of current agreements is available from the Engineering Council.

blocks.html: The assessors must complete a summary report, or reports, covering each component of the Professional Review, with a recommendation for each applicant. The report or reports must set out the assessors’ professional judgment of whether the applicant has demonstrated the competence and commitment required by the standard at the appropriate level.

blocks.html:
The decision whether or not to accept an applicant for registration must be made by the Licensee’s committee responsible for registration. The committee must base its decision on the reports from the Professional Review, against the standard adopted by the Licensee under V5-012. Its decisions, including recommendations, justifications, feedback and moderation, must be documented, transparent and auditable. Details of any international agreements or regulations applied and exemptions given must be recorded.

The committee must not award a registration title unless both assessors recommend it. Each Licensee must have a procedure for cases where the decision is not to accept an applicant on the basis of the Professional Review reports. The committee may recommend that the applicant repeat one or more components. Conditional passes are not permitted.

blocks.html: Licensees must inform the applicant of the outcome and, if unsuccessful, advise them about appropriate action to address deficiencies.
blocks.text: Licensees must inform the applicant of the outcome and, if unsuccessful, advise them about appropriate action to address deficiencies.

blocks.html:
Each Licensee must have an appeals procedure available to unsuccessful applicants. Unsuccessful applicants may appeal against the legitimacy of the process followed during the review of UKU and/or Professional Review, but not against the decision itself. Appeals must be considered by an Appeals Committee composed of registrants who did not materially participate in the appellant’s Professional Review.

An Appeals Committee may recommend that the applicant repeat one or more components of the Professional Review, but may not summarily reverse the recommendation of an earlier assessment. The final decision remains with the committee responsible for registration.

blocks.html: Programmes of learning include degrees, apprenticeships, national and vocational learning, and other qualifications, including those led by employers and Licensees. Recognition means that a programme fully or partially delivers the learning outcomes and/or delivers some or all of the competences for the relevant category of the Register set out in UK-SPEC.

blocks.html: Recognition may take the form of approval or accreditation. These are used to recognise programmes that provide all or some of the underpinning knowledge and understanding and/or develop competence for eventual registration in a particular category.

blocks.html: Licensees must hold the relevant licence to recognise programmes for registration purposes. Licensees that recognise programmes must appoint a committee responsible for recognition, which decides whether a programme will be recognised on the basis of the report of the accreditation or approval panel. Licensees must assess programmes against the learning outcomes in AHEP and AAQA, or against their own learning outcomes derived from and meeting those in AHEP and AAQA.
blocks.text: Licensees must hold the relevant licence to recognise programmes for registration purposes. Licensees that recognise programmes must appoint a committee responsible for recognition, which decides whether a programme will be recognised on the basis of the report of the accreditation or approval panel. Licensees must assess programmes against the learning outcomes in AHEP and AAQA, or against their own learning outcomes derived from and meeting those in AHEP and AAQA.

blocks.html: Recognition may attest to acquisition of both competence and underpinning knowledge and understanding, for example in integrated programmes. Licensees recognising such programmes must adopt competence statements derived from and meeting those in AAQA.
blocks.text: Recognition may attest to acquisition of both competence and underpinning knowledge and understanding, for example in integrated programmes. Licensees recognising such programmes must adopt competence statements derived from and meeting those in AAQA.

blocks.html:
Licensees undertaking recognition must establish detailed criteria and procedures, whether applied alone or through a joint board (DEF-008), specifying:

  • selection and training of assessors;
  • constitution of panels;
  • a balance of academic and industry assessors;
  • reasonable steps to avoid conflicts of interest;
  • panel experience relevant to the registration category;
  • the required provider submission;
  • any charges;
  • outline visit agendas;
  • judgment criteria, including mapped learning outcomes;
  • further consultation, decisions and feedback; and
  • the processes by which appeals against decisions may be considered, and
  • notification of decisions to the Engineering Council.
blocks.text: Licensees undertaking recognition must establish detailed criteria and procedures, whether applied alone or through a joint board (DEF-008), specifying: selection and training of assessors; constitution of panels; a balance of academic and industry assessors; reasonable steps to avoid conflicts of interest; panel experience relevant to the registration category; the required provider submission; any charges; outline visit agendas; judgment criteria, including mapped learning outcomes; further consultation, decisions and feedback; and the processes by which appeals against decisions may be considered, and notification of decisions to the Engineering Council.

blocks.html:
In making a judgment, Licensees must consider evidence from a range of indicators, including:

  • programme learning outcomes;
  • teaching and learning processes;
  • assessment strategies;
  • human, physical and material resources;
  • quality assurance arrangements;
  • feedback from students;
  • responses to previous recommendations and requirements; and
  • entry to the programme and support for cohort entry extremes.

For degree accreditation, evidence must include the awarding institution’s regulations on progression and awards. For approval of a formal qualification, evidence must include clearly defined, appropriately technical outcomes and satisfactory quality assurance arrangements.

For degree accreditation, evidence must include the awarding institution’s regulations on progression and awards. For approval of a formal qualification, evidence must include clearly defined, appropriately technical outcomes and satisfactory quality assurance arrangements.

blocks.html: Any decision by a Licensee to recognise a programme for which it is itself the awarding institution must be submitted to the Registration Standards Committee for authorisation.
blocks.text: Any decision by a Licensee to recognise a programme for which it is itself the awarding institution must be submitted to the Registration Standards Committee for authorisation.

blocks.html:
In considering applications for recognition, Licensees must:

  • recognise only programmes providing awards based on clearly defined learning outcomes;
  • ensure the programme is at an appropriate level in the applicable UK or international qualifications framework;
  • monitor the accuracy of published information about recognition status and registration;
  • visit the awarding institution if necessary; and
  • ensure that, where recognition attests to acquisition of competence, the programme covers the relevant competence standards in UK-SPEC or AAQA.

blocks.html: For accreditation of engineering degree programmes, Licensees must ensure that all students achieve all AHEP learning outcomes regardless of options taken, and the maximum credits permitted as 'failed' by university regulations. Evidence must be provided before accreditation. Condonement of modules delivering AHEP learning outcomes is not allowed. Compensation limits apply, major project modules must not be compensated, and the minimum compensated mark must be no more than ten percentage points below the nominal pass mark or equivalent.

blocks.html: A programme may be recognised as fully or partially meeting the learning outcomes at the requisite level. Recognition that partially meets the learning outcomes ('partial recognition') means that a recognised programme delivers a defined subset of the required learning outcomes and underpinning knowledge specified for a particular professional title. It confirms that the programme delivers part of the underpinning knowledge and understanding required for a category of registration, and that holders will need to demonstrate the remainder by other means (UKU-008).

blocks.html: Recognition may cover underpinning knowledge and understanding only or, for integrated programmes, competence as well (V5-036).
blocks.text: Recognition may cover underpinning knowledge and understanding only or, for integrated programmes, competence as well (V5-036).

blocks.html:
The committee responsible for recognition must decide to:

  • recognise the programme;
  • recognise the programme subject to specified constraints and/or specified modifications within a set timetable (V5-079); or
  • not recognise the programme.

Where it recognises a programme, the committee must state whether the programme fully or partially meets the learning outcomes at the requisite level, and whether it additionally meets, fully or partially, the competence requirement for the relevant category of UK-SPEC.

blocks.html: Where the committee grants recognition subject to constraints or modifications, the Licensee must specify them, and the timetable for meeting them, in its decision, and must notify the Engineering Council about any constraints which would restrict the eligibility of award holders.

blocks.html: Licensees must recognise programmes for a fixed period of not more than five years.
blocks.text: Licensees must recognise programmes for a fixed period of not more than five years.

blocks.html: Where a recognised programme’s curriculum does not change during the five-year period, the Licensee may renew recognition if it is satisfied that the programme remains relevant and meets the required standards.

blocks.html: In exceptional circumstances, a Licensee may extend recognition by a maximum of one year, once per recognition period, without a full renewal process. Before doing so, the Licensee must satisfy itself, and record, that the risk of extending recognition is acceptable.

blocks.html: Recognition may be backdated to allow cohorts whose work was reviewed as part of the recognition process to benefit. Backdating should apply immediately before forward recognition. Earlier backdating may be considered for RSC authorisation case by case; decisions must be documented, transparent and auditable.

blocks.html: Licensees must add all programmes they recognise to the Engineering Council’s recognised qualifications database, and must ensure that the data they have listed is current, complete and accurate. Recognition outside these Regulations must be authorised by RSC before database entry.

blocks.html: Licensees may remove recognition from a programme before the end of the recognition period, in which case they must update the recognised qualifications database promptly and alert the Engineering Council as early as possible. They must also require the awarding organisation or provider to notify affected individuals, explaining support available, implications for future registration and anything additional they must achieve.

blocks.html: The accreditation process must include a visit to the delivery site. Visits may be remote in certain circumstances. Where the same programme is delivered at multiple sites, the Licensee must satisfy itself that standards are met at each site for which accreditation applies; additional visits may be required.

The decision applies only to that exercise and must be recorded.

The detailed conditions for waiving a visit are set out in AHEP and AAQA.

blocks.html: The nature, purpose and value of IPD, and the processes for accrediting structured IPD schemes, are described in the IPD Policy Statement.
blocks.text: The nature, purpose and value of IPD, and the processes for accrediting structured IPD schemes, are described in the IPD Policy Statement.

blocks.html: Accreditation of an IPD scheme is the formal recognition that a provider's scheme provides engineers or technicians with the opportunity to develop and demonstrate the competence and commitment required by the applicable UK-SPEC standard, enabling them to apply for Professional Review.
blocks.text: Accreditation of an IPD scheme is the formal recognition that a provider's scheme provides engineers or technicians with the opportunity to develop and demonstrate the competence and commitment required by the applicable UK-SPEC standard, enabling them to apply for Professional Review.

blocks.html: Licensees must hold the relevant licence to accredit IPD schemes.
blocks.text: Licensees must hold the relevant licence to accredit IPD schemes.

blocks.html: A Licensee that accredits IPD schemes must publish and maintain documented policies, procedures and criteria for accreditation.
blocks.text: A Licensee that accredits IPD schemes must publish and maintain documented policies, procedures and criteria for accreditation.

blocks.html:
Licensees holding a licence to accredit an IPD scheme must:

  • publish criteria against which IPD schemes will be assessed;
  • define the information and evidence required from providers seeking accreditation;
  • recruit, train and approve suitably competent accreditation assessors;
  • define the standards and methods used to assess applications;
  • document the accreditation process, including accreditation visits;
  • ensure that accreditation decisions are based on an auditable peer review process (V5-074);
  • define the range of possible accreditation outcomes;
  • define how accreditation recommendations, judgements and decisions are reached and recorded; and
  • maintain records of accreditation activity and decisions.
blocks.text: Licensees holding a licence to accredit an IPD scheme must: publish criteria against which IPD schemes will be assessed; define the information and evidence required from providers seeking accreditation; recruit, train and approve suitably competent accreditation assessors; define the standards and methods used to assess applications; document the accreditation process, including accreditation visits; ensure that accreditation decisions are based on an auditable peer review process (V5-074); define the range of possible accreditation outcomes; define how accreditation recommendations, judgements and decisions are reached and recorded; and maintain records of accreditation activity and decisions.

blocks.html:
To be accredited, an IPD scheme must demonstrate that it:

  • is structured, documented and implemented;
  • provides participants with a clear understanding of the requirements for professional registration, including:
    • underpinning knowledge and understanding (where applicable);
    • competence development against the relevant UK-SPEC standard; and
    • preparation for Professional Review;
  • provides opportunities for participants to achieve the relevant UK-SPEC competence and commitment requirements;
  • identifies the sites, functions or activities through which participants can gain the required experience and evidence;
  • has visible support from senior management;
  • defines clear roles, responsibilities and accountabilities for the operation and delivery of the scheme;
  • provides access to appropriate guidance and mentoring;
  • operates suitable quality assurance and continuous improvement processes;
  • maintains records that demonstrate participant progress and achievement against the relevant UK-SPEC standard; and
  • provides each participant with a portable record of achievement that contains sufficient evidence for use at Professional Review with any Licensee.
blocks.text: To be accredited, an IPD scheme must demonstrate that it: is structured, documented and implemented; provides participants with a clear understanding of the requirements for professional registration, including: underpinning knowledge and understanding (where applicable); competence development against the relevant UK-SPEC standard; and preparation for Professional Review; provides opportunities for participants to achieve the relevant UK-SPEC competence and commitment requirements; identifies the sites, functions or activities through which participants can gain the required experience and evidence; has visible support from senior management; defines clear roles, responsibilities and accountabilities for the operation and delivery of the scheme; provides access to appropriate guidance and mentoring; operates suitable quality assurance and continuous improvement processes; maintains records that demonstrate participant progress and achievement against the relevant UK-SPEC standard; and provides each participant with a portable record of achievement that contains sufficient evidence for use at Professional Review with any Licensee.

blocks.html:
As a minimum, the scheme must define responsibilities for:

  • a Scheme Sponsor;
  • a Scheme Manager or Scheme Owner;
  • Line Managers;
  • Mentors; and
  • Participants.
blocks.text: As a minimum, the scheme must define responsibilities for: a Scheme Sponsor; a Scheme Manager or Scheme Owner; Line Managers; Mentors; and Participants.

blocks.html: The Licensee must ensure that any accreditation visit is undertaken by a suitably trained accreditation panel and that the outcomes, findings and decisions are recorded.

blocks.html: Where a scheme is delivered at more than one site or provider, the Licensee must satisfy itself that standards are met at each location for which accreditation will apply.

blocks.html: Licensees may carry out a remote visit to re-accredit an IPD scheme, but must first undertake a risk assessment to inform a decision on whether an in-person element to the visit is required.

blocks.html: The Licensee must retain sufficient evidence to demonstrate compliance with its accreditation process and published criteria.
blocks.text: The Licensee must retain sufficient evidence to demonstrate compliance with its accreditation process and published criteria.

blocks.html: Licensees may undertake accreditation assessment visits jointly with other Licensees where appropriate (a joint visit, DEF-009). Each Licensee must make its own decision on whether to accredit the scheme.

blocks.html: The nature, purpose and value of CPD for practising engineers, together with further information to support Licensees in meeting these requirements, are set out in the CPD Policy Statement. Further guidance on CPD sampling is provided in the Guidance Note on CPD Sampling, and additional guidance on removal from the Register is also available.

Further guidance on CPD sampling is provided in the Guidance Note on CPD Sampling, and additional guidance on removal from the Register is also available.

blocks.html:
Licensees must establish and implement appropriate policies and practices to support registrants in maintaining and enhancing their professional competence through continuing professional development (CPD). In particular, Licensees must:

  • establish and periodically review an appropriate CPD policy;
  • promote to registrants and employers the purpose, importance and benefits of CPD;
  • encourage access to development opportunities that meet the needs of registrants;
  • provide guidance and support to help registrants gain value from their CPD activities; and
  • provide registrants with a system that they may use for planning, recording, reviewing and sharing their CPD.
blocks.text: Licensees must establish and implement appropriate policies and practices to support registrants in maintaining and enhancing their professional competence through continuing professional development (CPD). In particular, Licensees must: establish and periodically review an appropriate CPD policy; promote to registrants and employers the purpose, importance and benefits of CPD; encourage access to development opportunities that meet the needs of registrants; provide guidance and support to help registrants gain value from their CPD activities; and provide registrants with a system that they may use for planning, recording, reviewing and sharing their CPD.

blocks.html: Licensees must review a representative sample of not less than 5% of their Engineering Council registrants’ CPD records annually, and must provide appropriate feedback to those sampled.
blocks.text: Licensees must review a representative sample of not less than 5% of their Engineering Council registrants’ CPD records annually, and must provide appropriate feedback to those sampled.

blocks.html: Licensees must have a process in place for considering requests for exemption from the CPD review where registrants were not professionally active during the period covered by the sample, or can demonstrate extenuating circumstances that prevented them from maintaining their CPD records. Decisions to grant an exemption rest with the Licensee.
blocks.text: Licensees must have a process in place for considering requests for exemption from the CPD review where registrants were not professionally active during the period covered by the sample, or can demonstrate extenuating circumstances that prevented them from maintaining their CPD records. blocks.html: Licensees must have arrangements in place to allow registrants who maintain a CPD record for their employer or another body to submit that record for review. The submission of a CPD record maintained elsewhere does not provide grounds for exemption from the Licensee’s CPD review.

blocks.html: Licensees must adopt and implement a policy and process for the removal from the Register of individuals who persistently fail to respond to, or engage with, requests to provide a CPD record.
